chief_complaint: slow growth, weight gain, and tiredness
hpi_details: 9-year-old female brought by parents due to poor growth and recent weight gain. Previously tracking on the 50th centile for height, she has dropped to below the 3rd centile over the past 2 years, growing only 2 cm last year. She has gained weight despite eating normally. She has also been increasingly tired, feels cold easily, complains of constipation and dry skin, and her school grades have been slipping recently. Her parents' heights are average.
ideas: parents think she might not be eating enough of the right foods for growing
concerns: parents are worried her poor growth and slipping grades mean something is seriously wrong with her brain or development
expectations: want vitamins or growth hormone to help her catch up
social_hx: Attends elementary school, grades recently slipping. Lives with parents.

boundaries_and_exceptions: While Hashimoto's is the most common cause, other etiologies of central hypothyroidism (e.g., craniopharyngioma) must be considered if TSH is not appropriately elevated despite low free T4.
In cases of severe, long-standing hypothyroidism, bone age may be markedly delayed, and rapid catch-up growth upon treatment initiation may lead to a disproportionate advancement in bone age.
common_misconceptions: Attributing the child's poor growth and fatigue solely to nutritional deficiencies or poor lifestyle habits, ignoring the paradox of weight gain.
Failing to recognize that acquired hypothyroidism in children often presents primarily with growth failure and a decline in academic performance rather than overt myxedema.
Overlooking the importance of plotting historical growth data to identify the point of growth deceleration.
Prescribing growth hormone empirically for short stature without ruling out hypothyroidism, which is a contraindication and will not work if the child is hypothyroid.
core_concepts: Growth deceleration in a child, especially when accompanied by weight gain, strongly suggests an endocrine etiology rather than a nutritional or chronic systemic disease.

Acquired primary hypothyroidism is most commonly caused by Hashimoto autoimmune thyroiditis and typically presents insidiously with growth failure, fatigue, cold intolerance, and declining school performance.
Initial evaluation of growth deceleration requires plotting current and historical heights on a growth chart, calculating growth velocity, and determining mid-parental target height.
Prompt initiation of levothyroxine replacement therapy is necessary to restore euthyroidism, normalize metabolism, and allow for catch-up growth.
dangerous_errors: Missing the diagnosis, leading to irreversible loss of adult height potential due to prolonged hypothyroidism and delayed bone age.
Failing to evaluate the child's cognitive decline, mislabeling it as a behavioral issue or learning disability.
Initiating excessive initial doses of levothyroxine in severe longstanding hypothyroidism, risking thyrotoxicosis or pseudotumor cerebri.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: slow growth, weight gain, and tiredness

Key HPI features: Height dropped from 50th centile to below 3rd centile over 2 years (severe growth deceleration, only 2 cm/year). Weight gain despite poor linear growth. Symptoms of metabolic slowing (fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin). Neurocognitive impact (slipping grades). Family history of maternal thyroid disease.
Relevant background/PMH: No prior chronic illness. Normal dietary intake.
management_principles: Perform basic auxologic evaluation: plot height and weight on growth charts, calculate growth velocity, and calculate mid-parental height.
Obtain screening laboratory tests for suspected hypothyroidism: serum TSH, free T4, and anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) or anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.
Obtain a left hand and wrist radiograph to assess bone age, which is characteristically delayed in hypothyroidism.
Initiate levothyroxine replacement therapy once the diagnosis is confirmed, and refer to pediatric endocrinology for ongoing management and monitoring of catch-up growth.

source_refs.title: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) - Clinical Practice Guidelines

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acquired primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto thyroiditis) in childhood

reference_soap.assessment: Acquired primary hypothyroidism, likely secondary to Hashimoto thyroiditis, presenting with significant growth deceleration and metabolic slowing.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 60 (bradycardia), RR 18, Temp 36.2C. Growth parameters show height dropping from 50th to <3rd centile over 2 years, weight increasing from 50th to 85th centile. General: Appears tired, slightly pale, and overweight for height. Skin: Dry and cool to touch. Neck: Possible small, firm, non-tender goiter. Neuro: Delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Plot all available height and weight data on a growth chart; calculate mid-parental height. 2. Order serum TSH, free T4, and thyroid autoantibodies (anti-TPO, anti-Tg). 3. Obtain a bone age radiograph of the left hand and wrist. 4. Plan to initiate levothyroxine once biochemical confirmation is obtained. 5. Refer to Pediatric Endocrinology for comprehensive management of thyroid replacement and monitoring of catch-up growth.
reference_soap.subjective: 9-year-old girl presenting with a 2-year history of poor growth (only 2 cm last year) and weight gain. She also complains of fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, and dry skin. Mother reports her school grades have recently dropped. Family history is significant for maternal thyroid disease.

learning_objectives: Identify growth deceleration combined with weight gain as a hallmark of endocrine pathology, specifically hypothyroidism.
Elicit a comprehensive history for symptoms of acquired hypothyroidism in children, including metabolic, cutaneous, and cognitive changes.
Understand the essential initial diagnostic workup for childhood hypothyroidism, including TSH, free T4, thyroid antibodies, and bone age assessment.
Formulate an appropriate initial management plan involving levothyroxine therapy and pediatric endocrinology referral.

must_ask.objective: Establish the pattern of growth over time
must_ask.say: Do you have her past growth records, and how much has she grown over the last year?
Has her weight changed recently, even with her slow growth?
Has she been feeling unusually tired, cold, or having trouble with constipation?
Have you noticed any changes in her school grades, memory, or focus?

must_ask.objective: Check for family history of autoimmune or endocrine disorders
must_ask.say: Does anyone in the family have thyroid problems or autoimmune diseases?

must_ask.objective: Determine parents' heights for target height calculation
must_ask.say: How tall are both of her parents?

teaching.one_liner: 9-year-old girl with growth deceleration, weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance, and declining school performance.
red_flags: Weight gain out of proportion to linear growth

history.answer: She is the shortest child in her class and does not seem to be growing at all lately.
We realized about two years ago that her clothes and shoes never needed sizing up, and she only grew two centimeters this past year.
Her doctor's charts showed she was right on the 50th percentile until age seven, but she has dropped completely below the 3rd percentile.
She has gained about five kilograms over the last year despite eating the same regular meals as the rest of us.
She eats normal portions of balanced meals, drinks plenty of water, and does not eat excessive snacks or sweets.
She has become exhausted all the time, falling asleep on the sofa after school and struggling to stay awake.
She always wears a thick sweater even indoors during warm weather and constantly complains that the house is freezing.
She has had hard, pellet-like stools only twice a week for several months, which is completely new for her.
Her skin has turned very dry and rough, and her hair feels coarser and tangles more easily.
She does not have any headaches, nausea, vomiting, or blurry vision.
She drinks normal amounts of water and does not wake up at night to urinate.
She has no chronic stomach aches, diarrhea, or blood in her stool.
She has not shown any signs of puberty yet, such as breast buds or body hair.
She sat up without support at six months and walked independently before her first birthday.
She babbled early, spoke her first clear words at eleven months, and spoke in full sentences by age two.
She has always made great eye contact, enjoyed playing with other children, and showed no repetitive or unusual behaviors.
She passed her newborn hearing screen, responds promptly to whispers, and has never had ear infections.
She has not lost any physical abilities or spoken words that she had previously mastered.
Her grades used to be mostly A's, but over the last few months her teachers noticed she is sluggish and struggling to concentrate.
She was born full term at 39 weeks weighing 3.2 kilograms after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and had no newborn nursery stays.
I am 162 centimeters tall and my husband is 175 centimeters tall, both of us entered puberty at normal ages, and neither side has hereditary dwarfism.
I have an underactive thyroid caused by Hashimoto's disease and take levothyroxine daily, but no one else has endocrine problems.
She has never taken daily steroid pills, steroid creams, asthma puffers, or ADHD medications.
She has always been generally healthy and has never been diagnosed with any chronic pediatric illnesses.
She has never undergone any surgical procedures and has never been admitted to a hospital.
She is not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, herbal remedies, or vitamins.
She has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or environmental triggers.
She lives at home with both of us in a smoke-free apartment, with no major family stressors.
All of her childhood immunizations are fully up to date according to the national schedule.
We were wondering whether her poor growth might be due to missing certain vitamins or nutrients in her food.
We are really worried that her stunted growth along with her slipping school grades might mean a serious brain condition.
We were hoping to find out what is causing this and whether growth hormone therapy or special vitamins could help her catch up.

exam.finding: Appears tired, slightly pale, and overweight for her height, with no dysmorphic facial features.
Blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, heart rate 60 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.2°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Height is 120 cm (below 3rd percentile, down from 50th), weight is 32 kg (85th percentile), with normal upper-to-lower body segment ratio.
Skin is noticeably cool, dry, and rough to the touch, without striae, rashes, or bruising.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable.
Slightly enlarged, firm, diffuse, non-tender thyroid gland palpable without discrete nodules or audible bruits.
Regular bradycardia at 60 beats per minute, normal S1 and S2, with no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds and no wheezing or crackles.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and mildly distended, with normal bowel sounds and no palpable liver or spleen enlargement.
Tanner stage 1 with prepubertal breast contour and no palpable breast buds or tenderness.
Tanner stage 1 female external genitalia with no pubic hair, clitoromegaly, or abnormal discharge.
Deep tendon reflexes present bilaterally with a markedly delayed relaxation phase in the patellar and Achilles reflexes.
